title: Voltage & Electric Potential
summary: Voltage is the electrical potential difference between two points that exerts pressure on electric charges, forcing them to flow through a circuit.

body.definition: The work required per unit charge (V = W/Q) to move a test charge between two points in an electric field, measured in Volts (V).

body.text: Using a water pipe analogy, voltage is equivalent to the water pressure generated by a pump or water tower. Higher voltage pushes more electrical charge through a given resistance per second, enabling work such as powering an LED or driving a computer processor.
Common Standard Voltages

items: 0.8V - 1.3V: Modern computer CPU/GPU core operational logic levels.
3.3V & 5.0V: Standard microcontroller logic rails (TTL/CMOS, Arduino, USB 2.0).
12.0V: Computer PSU main power rails (ATX12V, PCIe graphics power, cooling fans).
110V / 230V AC: Household mains electrical wall sockets.

body.text: Voltage is always measured relative between two points (differential), commonly referenced against a common circuit ground (0V).

title: Electric Current
summary: Electric current is the continuous net flow of electrical charge (electrons) through a conductive material, measured in Amperes (Amps).

body.definition: The rate at which electric charge flows through a cross-section of a conductor (I = dQ/dt), measured in Amperes (1 Ampere = 1 Coulomb per second).

body.text: In the water analogy, current represents the physical volume of water flowing through the pipe per second (liters/second). In electrical conductors, current is carried by the drift of mobile valence electrons moving in response to an applied voltage field.
Conventional Current vs Electron Flow

rows.label: Conventional Current
values: Established by Benjamin Franklin before electrons were discovered; used in all circuit schematics

rows.label: Actual Electron Flow
values: Electrons carry negative charge and are physically attracted toward the positive anode

body.text: High current through a conductor generates resistive heating proportional to I^2 * R (Joule Heating), which is why high-draw computer components require thick copper traces and heatsinks.

title: Electrical Resistance & Ohm's Law
summary: Resistance is the measure of an object opposition to the flow of electric current, mathematically relating voltage and current via Ohm's Law.

body.definition: The property of a material that opposes the passage of electric current, converting electrical energy into heat, measured in Ohms (Ω).

body.text: In the water pipe analogy, resistance corresponds to pipe friction or narrow constrictions that restrict flow. Ohm's Law states that current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance: V = I * R.
Ohm's Law Formulas

rows.label: Current (I)
values: Determining current draw through a known load

rows.label: Resistance (R)
values: Sizing a current-limiting resistor for an LED

rows.label: Power (P)
values: Calculating component heat dissipation in Watts

body.text: Superconductors cooled below their critical temperature exhibit exactly zero electrical resistance, allowing current to circulate indefinitely without energy loss.

title: Electrical Circuits
summary: An electrical circuit is a closed conductive loop providing a return path for electric current to flow continuously from a power source through components back to ground.

body.definition: An interconnected network of electrical components (power sources, resistors, switches, capacitors) forming at least one closed conductive loop.

body.text: If a conductive path is broken or disconnected at any single point, the circuit is 'Open' and zero current can flow. When unbroken, current circulates through active loads, performing electrical work before returning to the low-potential source terminal.
Series vs Parallel Topologies

rows.label: Series Circuit
values: Total voltage divided across components (V_total = V1 + V2)
If one component fails open, entire circuit halts

rows.label: Parallel Circuit
values: Current divides across branches (I_total = I1 + I2)
Full source voltage applied across every parallel branch
If one branch breaks, other branches continue operating

body.text: A 'Short Circuit' occurs when low-resistance wires bypass the intended load, causing massive current spikes that blow fuses, trip circuit breakers, or ignite fires.

title: Transistors & Semiconductor Logic
summary: A transistor is a three-terminal semiconductor device that amplifies electrical signals or acts as a microscopic binary switch.

body.definition: A solid-state semiconductor component that uses voltage or current applied to a control terminal to regulate current flowing between two other terminals.

body.text: The transistor is the foundational invention of modern digital technology. By applying a tiny voltage to the Gate terminal of a MOSFET (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor), the conductive channel between Source and Drain opens or closes, representing binary 1 or 0.
From Transistors to Modern Microprocessors

items: Logic Gates: Pairing NMOS and PMOS transistors (CMOS) creates fundamental logic gates (NAND, NOR, NOT, AND, OR).
Arithmetic Logic Units (ALU): Combining thousands of logic gates creates adders, multipliers, and registers.
Modern CPU Density: A modern smartphone SoC (like Apple A17 Pro or Snapdragon 8 Elite) packs over 15 to 20 billion microscopic transistors onto a single silicon chip.

body.text: Modern transistor gates in sub-3nm semiconductor fabrication nodes are only a few atoms wide, requiring FinFET and Gate-All-Around (GAA) nanosheet structures to prevent quantum tunneling leakage.

title: Capacitors & Energy Storage
summary: A capacitor is a passive two-terminal electronic component that stores electrical energy in an electrostatic field between conductive plates separated by a dielectric insulator.

body.definition: A passive component that accumulates and stores electric charge (Q = C * V) across an internal dielectric barrier, measured in Farads (F).

body.text: While batteries store energy chemically and release it slowly, capacitors store energy physically in an electrostatic field and can charge or discharge in microseconds. In computer circuits, capacitors act as local energy shock absorbers that smooth out power ripple.
Primary Engineering Applications

items: Decoupling / Bypass: Placed right next to CPU power pins to supply instantaneous bursts of current during sudden computational workloads, preventing voltage droop.
Power Filtering: Smoothing rectified AC ripple into clean DC voltage inside power supplies.
Signal Coupling: Passing high-frequency AC audio signals while blocking DC bias voltages.
DRAM Memory Cells: Each bit in computer RAM is stored as a minute electric charge on a microscopic microscopic capacitor.

body.text: Electrolytic capacitors are polarized and will violently rupture if connected with reverse polarity in a circuit.

title: Light Emitting Diodes (LED)
summary: An LED is a semiconductor p-n junction diode that emits incoherent narrow-spectrum light via electroluminescence when forward-biased.

body.definition: A semiconductor optoelectronic diode that emits photons when electrons recombine with electron holes across its forward-biased bandgap.

body.text: Unlike incandescent light bulbs (which waste 90% of electrical energy as heat by heating a tungsten filament), LEDs convert electrical energy directly into light photons with extreme efficiency and virtually zero heat degradation.
Bandgap & Color Spectrum

items: Forward Voltage (Vf): The threshold voltage needed to conduct (e.g. ~1.8V for Red, ~3.2V for Blue/White).
Photon Energy: The exact semiconductor compound (Gallium Nitride, Indium Gallium Phosphide) dictates the energy bandgap and color wavelength.
Current-Driven Device: LEDs have near-zero internal resistance once conducting; they always require a series current-limiting resistor or constant-current driver to prevent thermal runaway.

body.text: White LEDs are actually blue LEDs coated with an internal yellow cerium-doped YAG phosphor layer that absorbs part of the blue light and emits yellow, mixing to produce white light.

title: Resistors in Circuit Design
summary: A resistor is a passive two-terminal electronic component that implements precise electrical resistance to limit current, divide voltages, and pull logic pins.

body.definition: A foundational passive electronic component fabricated from carbon film, metal oxide, or wire windings to provide a fixed electrical resistance.

body.text: Resistors are the most numerous components on printed circuit boards. They govern current distribution, ensure input pins remain in known binary states, and dissipate excess electrical energy safely as heat.
Common Resistor Functions

rows.label: Current Limiting
values: Protects sensitive components like LEDs or microcontroller I/O pins from burnout

rows.label: Pull-Up / Pull-Down
values: Anchors high-impedance digital input pins to VCC or GND to prevent floating logic states

rows.label: Voltage Divider
values: Steps down a higher sensor voltage proportionally to be readable by an ADC

body.text: Through-hole resistors use standard 4-band or 5-band color codes to denote resistance value and manufacturing tolerance.

title: Alternating Current (AC) vs Direct Current (DC)
summary: DC flows unidirectionally in a constant direction, while AC periodically reverses direction and alternates polarity in a sinusoidal waveform.

body.definition: The two primary methods of electrical power transmission: DC maintains constant polarity, while AC oscillates direction periodically at a set frequency (50/60 Hz).

body.text: Power grids deliver AC electricity because high-voltage AC can be stepped up to hundreds of thousands of volts with transformers, allowing electricity to be transmitted across hundreds of miles with minimal resistance losses. However, all digital electronics (smartphones, computers, microchips) require steady, low-voltage DC.
AC vs DC Comparison

rows.label: Power Sources
values: Chemical batteries, solar panels, power supplies

rows.label: Transformation
values: Requires complex active DC-DC buck/boost switching converters
Easily stepped up or down with passive copper transformers

rows.label: Usage
values: Heavy industrial electric motors, long-distance grid transmission

body.text: A Rectifier (diode bridge) converts AC into pulsating DC, which is then filtered with capacitors and regulated into clean DC by switching regulators.

title: Computer Motherboards
summary: The motherboard is the primary printed circuit board (PCB) that houses the CPU, RAM, storage interfaces, expansion buses, and power delivery circuitry.

body.definition: The central multi-layer printed circuit board establishing electrical power routing and high-speed data interconnects between all core computer peripherals.

body.text: Modern motherboards contain up to 12 layers of fiberglass and copper traces sandwiched together. High-speed PCIe traces and memory channels must be matched down to fractions of a millimeter in trace length to prevent phase delay and signal crosstalk at gigahertz frequencies.
Critical Motherboard Subsystems

items: Voltage Regulator Module (VRM): Multi-phase switching buck converters that step down 12V PSU power to precise ~1.2V CPU core voltages.
Chipset: Hub silicon managing USB controllers, SATA ports, PCIe expansion routing, and audio codecs.
PCIe Slots: Direct high-speed lanes to CPU silicon for graphics cards and NVMe storage.
BIOS/UEFI SPI Flash: Persistent memory chip holding pre-boot firmware and hardware configuration.

body.text: Form factors (ATX, Micro-ATX, Mini-ITX) standardize motherboard mounting screw locations, rear I/O shield dimensions, and power connector pinouts.

title: Power Supply Units (PSU)
summary: A PSU is a Switched-Mode Power Supply (SMPS) that converts high-voltage AC mains power into regulated low-voltage DC rails (+12V, +5V, +3.3V) for computer components.

body.definition: An electrical converter that takes 110V/230V AC grid electricity, rectifies it, and uses high-frequency pulse-width modulation (PWM) to output stabilized DC voltage.

body.text: Modern computers use Switched-Mode Power Supplies (SMPS). Instead of dissipating excess voltage as heat like obsolete linear regulators, an SMPS switches power MOSFETs on and off tens of thousands of times per second, achieving energy conversion efficiencies exceeding 90%.
80 PLUS Efficiency Ratings
Modern power supplies include vital protection circuits: OVP (Over Voltage), OCP (Over Current), OPP (Over Power), and SCP (Short Circuit Protection).
